source.title: Automatically Finding Rule-Based Neurons in OthelloGPT
source.authors: Aditya Singh; Zihang Wen; Srujananjali Medicherla; Adam Karvonen; C. Rager

page_placements.theme: Rule-like neurons in small game- or task-trained models (OthelloGPT, Sudoku, DRL agents, numeric succession)

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how well neuron-level rule descriptions predict activations on held-out Othello game states, a different method and setting from the claim's explanation audits.
record.gate_note: The study reports a held-out decision-tree prediction result for layer 5 and causal ablation results for rule-targeted neurons. The baseline comparisons in Figures 2 and 3 are not extracted as rows because they compare explanation methods rather than report the claim's named neuron-explanation outcomes. Layer-wise intervention plots are described qualitatively in the text; exact plotted values are not stated.
record.test_reason: The study fits depth-4 regression decision trees from board-state features to OthelloGPT MLP neuron activations. It reports how many neurons the trees predict well on held-out games (R² > 0.7 for 913/2,048 in layer 5), plus causal ablations. That is a share of rule-describable neurons in a 25M game-move transformer, measured with a supervised surrogate. It is not a language model's neuron-pole audit (V1/V2). It is not a natural-language explanation fitted to activating examples (V6). It is not an explainer model's explanation scored by simulating activations on new text (V7). The authors state that their approach assumes neurons are the natural unit of analysis, and they report their method's performance against baselines. So the study uses the neuron-as-unit premise without testing any version. Its interpretable-share result is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that many OthelloGPT neurons follow compact logical rules aligned with game mechanics, and that intervening on them predictably alters behaviour. They add that this rule-like reasoning coexists with distributed, continuous computation that their trees only partly capture.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains supervised decision trees to predict OthelloGPT neuron activations from board features and tests them on game states; it does not use language-model-generated neuron explanations or the Qwen3 pole-audit procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on layer: the authors report rule-based neurons concentrated in layers 5–6 and subpar fine-grained intervention results for the 12 squares adjacent to the middle 2x2 region. The 48-square analysis excluding the middle 4x4 showed stronger intervention-control differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth-4 regression decision trees predict held-out activations with R² > 0.7 for 913 of 2,048 layer-5 OthelloGPT MLP neurons (about 45%). Rule-describable neurons are concentrated in layers 5–6. The authors attribute the remainder to distributed or non-rule-based computation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small game-trained transformer, roughly half of the neurons in the most rule-like layer are well predicted by compact rule-based surrogates, and fewer elsewhere.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating neurons surfaced for a target legal-move pattern degrades that pattern about 2x more than a control pattern on mean probability. The gap is about 4–10x on the below-1% metric. The effects are incomplete.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rule-identified OthelloGPT neurons have pattern-specific but incomplete causal effects on legal-move prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing rule-based neurons (R² > 0.7) with their tree outputs keeps accuracy high and KL low. Zero or mean ablation of the same neurons drops performance sharply, most in layers 5–6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decision-tree surrogates of selected OthelloGPT neurons preserve much of their function.

record.problems: The study covers only OthelloGPT and focuses on rule-based behavior. Its depth-4 trees may miss long conjunctions or continuous features, and the authors note that computations may be distributed across neuron groups or attention heads. The fine-grained intervention effects are incomplete. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Numerical values from Figures 2–4 and Figure 6 were not transcribed where the paper did not state them in text; Figure 4's qualitative layer-wise outcomes are recorded in R34–R35.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no one-job / two-job / not-understood shares.
No language models, no dense versus mixture-of-experts comparison, no scale sweep.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic-neuron reanalysis; no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No manipulation of architecture, regularization or tool quality, and no vision models.
No neuron-based attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No explanations fitted to activating examples by inspection, and no check of whether such explanations predict firing.
No explainer-model natural-language explanations and no simulation scoring on new text.

missing.what: Per-layer counts of neurons above R² cutoffs of 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 (regression trees) and above F1 cutoffs (binary trees), for layers 0–7. Only the layer-5 figure is stated in text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links of R1 to V6 and V7, and its limits_scope labels, are removed. The surrogate here is a supervised decision tree trained on ground-truth board features in a non-language game model. It is neither an inspection-based explanation nor a simulated-explanation score. The interpretable share also depends on tree depth (depth 4) and on the R² cutoff chosen. The control-row 'partial' states in R3–R33 carry no version meaning, since those rows are linked to no version.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimates of one-job, two-related-job, or not-understood shares.
No comparison across language-model architectures or scales, and no dense or mixture-of-experts model sweep.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No test of architecture, regularization, tool quality, or interpretability shares in vision models.
The study does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain a large model without a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
The study tests decision-tree predictors on held-out Othello board states, not explanations fitted to activating examples by inspection; it does not study modern language models.
No new-text evaluation or comparison of stronger explainer models; the tested explanations are decision trees for OthelloGPT activations.

rows.check: The row measures held-out R² of supervised decision-tree surrogates in OthelloGPT, a game-move transformer. The value itself (913 of 2,048, layer 5, R² > 0.7) is correctly transcribed.

rows.problem: none; no version links, and cannot_determine fits because no version covers rule-describability in OthelloGPT

relation.reason: The study does not assume that most neurons are interpretable. It measures the share and says the rest are likely distributed. The Limitations line says the approach assumes 'individual neurons are the natural unit of analysis'. That is a unit-of-analysis premise the authors flag as a limitation, not the claim. They discuss neuron-level coverage without testing a version.

tranche.reason: T4 needs a study that relies on the finding as a tool and reports only its own method's performance. This study does neither. It measures the share of rule-describable OthelloGPT neurons (about half of layer 5) and runs causal ablations. That share is a related but different construct, in a game-move transformer, and no version covers it. So it is not a test, and T6 fits.

source_check.notes: OthelloGPT (25M, trained on Othello moves), not a language-model neuron audit. 913/2,048 (44.6%) of layer-5 neurons reach R2 > 0.7 with depth-4 regression trees on ground-truth board features, a strict surrogate fit and not 'one main job'. The text does not state the regression R2 test split. Not a test of any version; belongs under fits_no_version.

statements.problem: The text has 913 of 2,048 neurons, layer 5, depth-4 regression trees and R2 > 0.7. 913/2,048 = 44.6%, so 'about 45%' is right; the authors say 'roughly half'. The Discussion says rule-based neurons concentrate in layers 5-6. Minor: 'held-out' is implied rather than stated for the regression R2. Appendix A gives a 500-game test set for the binary trees.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Layer 5 of OthelloGPT, regression decision trees on held-out board states
reader_labels.reason: The trees exceeded R² > 0.7 for 913 of 2,048 neurons, while the paper says the remaining neurons likely involve distributed or non-rule-based computations (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports roughly half of layer-5 neurons above its R² > 0.7 criterion, not a consistently high score across neurons; it does not test stronger explainer models or new text (R1).
